extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, logicians and cognitive scientists studying humor, nonmonotonic reasoning, and belief revision
extracted.subtask_description: Formalize when a two-part statement (<context>=α, <punchline>=β) can be considered a joke by modeling a listener as a belief-revising agent (K, ◦) using default reasoning and possibility/pre-order semantics. The paper gives formal definitions of surprise, revelation, potential funniness, and a way to encode incongruity as norm-violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising punchline (formal condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement (α, β) is surprising for a listener associated with (K, ◦) if (K ◦ α) is consistent and (K ◦ α) ∧ (K ◦ (α ∧ β)) |= ⊥.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes that the listener must be able to form an expectation from the context α (so K ◦ α consistent) and the punchline produces an inconsistency with that expectation. It excludes cases where the listener already knows the joke. The definition allows K ◦ (α ∧ β) to be inconsistent (nonsensical punchlines may be surprising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revealing punchline (formal condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline β is revealing for (K, ◦) if (K ◦ β) is consistent and K ◦ β |= α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revelation means that, once β is accepted, the initial context α becomes explained: 'if one had known β from the beginning, it would have explained α'. Revelation provides the cognitive resolution needed for relief (laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potentially funny statement (compositional criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is potentially funny for a listener associated with (K, ◦) if it is surprising and its punchline is revealing for this listener (Definition 4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential funniness depends on both the listener's knowledge base K and revision behaviour ◦ (so jokes can be audience-dependent). Being 'potentially funny' is necessary but not sufficient for actual laughter — other psychological, cultural and delivery factors matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listener must reason under incomplete information (nonmonotonic capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The capability of the listener to reason under incomplete information (use default/nonmonotonic reasoning) is necessary for understanding many jokes; a psycho-rigid (purely monotonic) listener cannot be surprised and hence 'is not open to laughing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the listener with a knowledge base Σ = (P, ∆) where ∆ is a set of default rules that induce a plausibility pre-order. Default inferences allow provisional conclusions from α that the punchline can later overturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of known jokes / prior knowledge condition
rubrics_metrics.description: If α and β are already deducible from K (the listener already knows the joke), no surprise can arise; the definition of surprise excludes this possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the listener's K does not already entail the context and punchline; practical implication: novelty to audience is required for the modeled surprise effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief revision rationality postulates (KM1–KM6 / AGM principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A revision operator ◦ must satisfy rationality postulates (Katsuno & Mendelzon / AGM): e.g., KM1 κ ◦ ϕ |= ϕ; KM2 if κ ∧ ϕ satisfiable then κ ◦ ϕ ≡ κ ∧ ϕ; KM3 if ϕ satisfiable then κ ◦ ϕ satisfiable; KM4 syntax independence; KM5/KM6 minimal change constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling jokes via belief revision requires a rational revision operator so that 'new information holds', minimal change is respected, consistency obtained when possible, and operator behavior corresponds to intuitive closeness/preference among interpretations. Use these postulates to justify the formal definitions of surprise and revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plausibility pre-orders and possibility distributions to implement revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision semantics are implemented by associating to the listener a total pre-order (≼_K) on interpretations (or equivalently a qualitative possibility distribution π). Then M od(K ◦ ϕ) = min(M od(ϕ), ≼_K) (representation theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encode default rules ∆ via constraints Π(α∧β) > Π(α∧¬β) to build π_∆ (least restrictive possibility distribution satisfying constraints). Use System Z, best-out ordering, or lexicographic ordering to stratify defaults and obtain pre-orders. This yields concrete computational criteria for when min(Mod(α), ≼) and min(Mod(α∧β), ≼) are disjoint (surprise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise degree metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise can be measured quantitatively by surpriseDegree(A) = 1 − possibility(A) (possibility theory formulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the possibility distribution π reflecting the listener's uncertainty to compute how 'surprising' a fact is: lower possibility → higher surprise. This provides a graded notion beyond the binary surprising/not-surprising definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity constraints and consistency with P
rubrics_metrics.description: The listener's knowledge base Σ = (P, ∆) may include strict/integrity rules P; revisions are performed under integrity constraints: K ◦_P ϕ = K ◦ (P ∪ {ϕ}); definitions typically assume α and β are consistent with P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling jokes, ensure α and β do not violate hard constraints P unless deliberately modeling norm violation; counterexamples of P are assigned lowest possibility (π_Σ) so that revisions respect P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as violation of norms encoded by defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity is modeled as violation of (social) norms: default rules representing norms (e.g., ¬knowEachOther → ¬together) are violated by the punchline/context, producing an incongruous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat norms as (high-priority) defaults or as rules in P; an incongruous punchline is one that is a revelation 'in disregard of' a norm (formally: non-monotonic entailment after removing a norm or showing the preferred models violate the norm). The model suggests encoding norms as defaults whose violation can be detected in the best-out or lexicographic ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree/level of incongruity influences comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic effect increases with how obvious or mandatory the disregarded social norm is; thus incongruity may have degrees linked to the 'shocking nature' of the non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed extension: introduce measures/levels of incongruity (e.g., weight/priority of norm defaults) so jokes violating high-priority norms produce stronger incongruity and potentially stronger comic effect — but may also shock and reduce laughter depending on audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity resolution requirement (make the initial thing acceptable)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Incongruity resolution' means finding a logic or reinterpreting the initial situation so it appears less incongruous (i.e., 'make it acceptable'); resolution plays an important role in laughter and in children's humor development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models should allow mechanisms by which the listener reinterprets α given β to reduce perceived incongruity (e.g., by altering applicability of defaults or context frame). Without some resolution that makes the situation comprehensible (even if still norm-violating), relief (laughter) is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsensical punchlines allowed for surprise but not for revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition allows nonsensical punchlines to be surprising (K ◦ (α ∧ β) may be inconsistent), but such nonsensical punchlines will typically fail to be revealing (hence not 'potentially funny').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish surprise from revelation: surprising alone does not suffice. For modeling potential funniness require both, so filter out purely nonsensical surprises when assessing potential jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling incongruity as exception to typical/default rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An exception to a default rule (a typical rule) can be interpreted as incongruous: e.g., violation of a typical rule R1 is detected by demonstrating a non-monotonic inference showing the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples where removing a rule R_i changes the preferred models so that the punchline becomes a revelation 'in disregard of' R_i. This gives a concrete test for incongruity in the default-rule framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and pragmatic factors matter (delivery, audience, cultural background)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a potentially funny statement actually produces laughter depends on teller adaptation, delivery, audience background, physiological/psychological/sociological/cultural dimensions, identification with characters, and adherence/violation of conversational maxims (e.g., Gricean maxims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal model supplies necessary structural/cognitive conditions (surprise + revelation ± incongruity) but evaluation of real-world funniness requires incorporating pragmatic models of teller/listener, multi-agent reasoning, and social context. Use caution when mapping formal potential to empirical laughter.
